To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) geodabs can serve as a basis for a distributed inverted index; 2) the probabilistic nature has a marginal effect; and 3) the quality of results does not deteriorate with increasing density of the trajectory data.

geodabs can: be used to build efficient and scalable inverted indexes for trajectory data; be normalized to improve the precision of the search results; be distributed to improve performances; and be used to efficiently discover motifs.
geodabs can efficiently and scalably be used to index trajectories and that the quality of the resulting indexes is not affected by dataset density.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach is the first to scale to dense trajectory datasets.
geodabs are a promising alternative to the state-of-the-art for trajectory indexing and similarity search.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we show how a technique that was originally conceived to detect plagiarism in textual data can be applied to trajectory data, thus enabling a new approach to the problem of finding similar trajectories in large datasets.
, by using a space filling curve and fingerprinting techniques, we are able to efficiently build sharded indexes that are resilient to data density.
we propose a novel approach for trajectory similarity search that can be efficiently distributed in large scale systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fingerprinting can be used to index trajectories at scale, and that the resulting inverted indexes can be used to efficiently retrieve similar trajectories.
, by relying on geodabs, it is possible to efficiently index and query dense datasets of trajectories.
, when it comes to similarity search, fingerprinting is a viable alternative to spatial indexing.
